topics.title: Ind-Aus Uranium Deal
bullets: In July 2026, India secured a long-term uranium supply deal with Australia, marking a key step towards operationalising the India- Australia Civil Nuclear Cooperation Agreement signed nearly 12 years ago .
The deal was finalised during the Third India-Australia Annual Summit in Melbourne on 9 July 2026, with both Prime Ministers Narendra Modi and Anthony Albanese overseeing the agreement .
The agreement comes as India pursues an ambitious target of expanding its civil nuclear power capacity to 100 gigawatt-electric (GWe) by 2047, requiring significant fuel imports . Background –
The Civil Nuclear Cooperation Agreement was signed between India and Australia in September 2014 and came into force in November 2015 .
Australia, which holds about one-third of the world's known recoverable uranium resources, had historically refused to export uranium to India due to India's non-signatory status to the NPT .
The 2008 NSG waiver ended India's "nuclear pariah" status, paving the way for the 2014 agreement .
On 9 July 2026, India and Australia finalised the Administrative Arrangement under the Civil Nuclear Cooperation Agreement, enabling long-term uranium exports .
The arrangement establishes procedures for implementing the agreement and provides a stable, long-term framework for cooperation between both governments and industry .
PM Modi described the agreement as a pathway that would "pave the way for uranium supplies from Australia to India and give our clean energy objectives fresh momentum" .
Australia possesses the largest uranium resources globally, accounting for more than one-third of the global total .
Under Australian policy, uranium is exported only to countries covered by a civil nuclear cooperation agreement, and all exports must be for exclusively peaceful purposes under IAEA safeguards .
Despite holding the world's largest uranium reserves, Australia has no commercial nuclear power industry due to laws enacted in the late 1990s .
Australia reaffirmed its support for India's membership of the Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG) as part of the deal .
This is significant because India is not a signatory to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) and requires NSG support for nuclear trade .
India had received a 'clean' NSG waiver in 2008, making it the only non-NPT signatory to enjoy such trading privileges .

India's domestic uranium oxide reserves currently stand at around 4.3 lakh tonnes, spread across 47 uranium deposits in Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Jharkhand, Meghalaya, Rajasthan, Karnataka, and other states .
Uranium Corp. of India Ltd (UCIL) operates major mines in Jaduguda and Turamdih in Jharkhand and Tummalapalle in Andhra Pradesh .
However, the uranium requirement for only 2.4 GWe out of 8.7 GWe capacity is currently met from domestic sources, with the rest coming from imports .
Mining and processing domestic uranium into uranium ore concentrate costs three to four times more than procuring it from international markets
The higher cost is mainly due to the poor grade of uranium ore found in India
A government committee recommended that "even if expensive, this will help to have a degree of energy security" and suggested infusing additional equity in UCIL
India currently imports uranium from Russia and Uzbekistan
Shipments from Canadian miner Cameco Corp. , under a $2.6 billion supply agreement signed in March 2026, are expected to begin in 2027
Kazakhstan's NAC Kazatomprom , the world's largest uranium producer, agreed in February 2026 to sell a substantial volume of uranium to India
India's largest power producer, NTPC, is seeking to invest in overseas uranium mines to secure supplies for the 30 GW of nuclear capacity it plans to build over the next two decades .
NTPC has issued a tender to appoint consultants to identify potential assets in uranium-mining countries including Canada, Australia, Kazakhstan and South Africa . SHANTI Act 2025 –
The Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India (SHANTI) Act, 2025 received presidential assent in December 2025 .
The Act repeals the Atomic Energy Act of 1962 and the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act of 2010, consolidating and modernising India's nuclear legal framework .
It enables private companies and joint ventures to build, own, operate and decommission nuclear power plants under a license from the government .
The Act allows foreign direct investment of up to 49% through joint ventures with Indian entities, while retaining majority ownership on the domestic side .
It removes statutory supplier liability and caps operator liability, aligning India's nuclear regime with global standards .
The Act supports India's clean-energy transition and the long-term objective of achieving 100 GW nuclear energy capacity by 2047 .
While the overall liability cap remains at ₹3,000 crore, the Act introduces graded limits linked to reactor size – smaller reactors will face significantly lower liability .
This replaces the earlier flat cap of ₹1,500 crore that applied uniformly to all plants above 10 MW .
The reforms are expected to boost investor confidence by making liability proportionate to the scale of the project .
The SHANTI Act is expected to enable private players such as the Adani Group, Larsen & Toubro, and Tata Power to enter India's nuclear sector .
However, most private energy companies in India lack experience in running nuclear plants, and NPCIL remains the only operator with proven expertise .
The government has allocated ₹20,000 crore in the latest Union Budget for the design, development, and deployment of Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) .
India's Nuclear Energy Mission targets 100 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047
This would account for about 10-11% of India's total electricity requirements, with renewables contributing around 70-75%
Nuclear power is seen as a reliable source of large-scale, low- carbon baseload electricity that complements the variable output of solar and wind Recent News –
The Third India-Australia Annual Summit was held in Melbourne on 9 July 2026, reaffirming the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership
The Summit delivered outcomes across maritime security, energy security, cyber cooperation, critical technologies, skill development and entrepreneurship
The Administrative Arrangement under the Civil Nuclear Cooperation Agreement was finalised at the Summit
Earlier in 2026, India signed similar long-term uranium supply agreements with Canada and Kazakhstan
The Canadian agreement with Cameco Corp. is worth $2.6 billion for 8,300 metric tonnes of uranium ore concentrate, with shipments beginning in 2027
The Kazakh agreement with Kazatomprom (the world's largest uranium producer) is expected to make Kazakhstan one of India's most significant uranium suppliers
On 6 April 2026, India's indigenously developed 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam attained first criticality .
The PFBR marks the beginning of the second stage of India's three-stage nuclear programme .
Unlike conventional reactors, the PFBR uses plutonium recovered from spent fuel and is designed to produce more nuclear fuel than it consumes, eventually breeding Uranium-233 from thorium .

The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) has issued siting consent for the Mahi Banswara Rajasthan Atomic Power Project 1 to 4, a greenfield project being developed by ASHVINI (a JV between NPCIL and NTPC) .
AERB has also approved fuel loading in the 500 MW Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor at Kalpakkam .
India has signed Inter-Governmental Agreements on civil nuclear cooperation with 18 countries for peaceful purposes .
India is developing indigenous Small Modular Reactors, including a light water-based 200 MWe Bharat SMR, a 55 MWe SMR, and a High Temperature Gas Cooled Reactor for clean hydrogen production .
The government has allocated USD 2 billion for R&D on SMRs, with a target to operationalise five indigenously designed SMRs by 2033 .
SMRs are seen as suitable for dense urban clusters, industrial corridors, and emerging economic zones .
High capital intensity: A typical 700 MW PHWR requires ₹20,000–28,000 crore investment, translating into ₹15– 18 crore per MW .
Long gestation periods: Vendor qualification cycles can take five to seven years .
Supply chain constraints: India's nuclear build-out faces structural constraints across manufacturing, financing and execution .

topics.title: BIMSTEC
bullets: BIMSTEC stands for the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi- Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation – a regional organisation comprising countries bordering the Bay of Bengal.
It seeks to act as a bridge between South Asia and Southeast Asia, fostering cooperation across multiple sectors.
As of 2026, BIMSTEC has seven member states and is approaching its 30th anniversary in June 2027. Background –
BIMSTEC was originally formed as BIST-EC (Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka, and Thailand Economic Cooperation) on 6 June 1997 in Bangkok.
The grouping was created mainly on the initiative of Thailand, first mooted in 1992-93.
The primary aim was the promotion of economic cooperation between countries bordering the Bay of Bengal.
Myanmar joined the grouping on 22 December 1997, following a special Ministerial Meeting in Bangkok.
With Myanmar's admission, the group was renamed BIMST- EC (Bangladesh, India, Myanmar, Sri Lanka, and Thailand Economic Cooperation).
This expanded the group's geographical reach, linking South Asia more closely with Southeast Asia.
Nepal and Bhutan joined BIMSTEC in February 2004, bringing the total membership to seven.
Following their admission, the group was renamed BIMSTEC – the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation.
This completed the current composition of the grouping.
A significant milestone was reached when the BIMSTEC Charter came into force in May 2024.
The Charter provides a formal institutional framework for the grouping, which previously operated without a legally binding foundational document.
India extended a Grant of USD 1 Million to the BIMSTEC Secretariat for institution building.
The seven BIMSTEC member states are: Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka, and Thailand.
The grouping includes five of the eight SAARC members, but notably excludes Pakistan.
This exclusion is significant as it allows BIMSTEC to avoid the political blockages that have paralysed SAARC.
The BIMSTEC Secretariat is located in Dhaka, Bangladesh.
The Secretary-General is Indra Mani Pandey, a senior Indian diplomat.
BIMSTEC will complete 30 years of its journey on 6 June 2027.
The BIMSTEC Permanent Working Committee (BPWC) is an institutional mechanism for administrative and financial supervision.
The BPWC meets regularly, with a meeting held in Dhaka on 7-8 April 2026.
It ensures the smooth operation of the Secretariat and coordination among member states. Objectives –
BIMSTEC aims to foster regional cooperation and promote socio- economic development through collaborative efforts in various sectors.
The grouping seeks to act as a bridge between South and Southeast Asia.
It focuses on sectoral partnerships rather than broad political integration.
BIMSTEC operates through 14 priority sectors of cooperation, including trade, investment, transport, energy, tourism, fisheries, agriculture, and disaster management.
Other sectors include counter-terrorism, cyber security, maritime security, health, and people-to-people contacts.
India has established the BIMSTEC Centre of Excellence for Disaster Management to cooperate in disaster management, relief, and rehabilitation in Gandhinagar, Gujarat.
BIMSTEC members have been engaged in Free Trade Agreement (FTA) talks, focusing on strengthening business-to-business linkages.
Together, BIMSTEC members have a combined GDP of nearly $5 trillion, representing significant economic potential.
The BIMSTEC Master Plan on Transport Connectivity is currently being updated to reflect evolving regional priorities.
The BIMSTEC Energy Centre has been established in Bengaluru, India.
The Host Country Agreement (HCA) was signed on 11 November 2024, paving the way for early operationalisation.
This is the second BIMSTEC regional centre hosted by India in the field of security. First is BIMSTEC Centre for Weather and Climate (BCWC), located in Noida, Uttar Pradesh. Recent News –
The 5th BIMSTEC National Security Chiefs' Meeting was held in New Delhi on 16 July 2026.
It was hosted and chaired by India's National Security Adviser Ajit Doval.
The meeting was attended by heads of delegation from all seven BIMSTEC member states.
Delegates discussed "practical and result-oriented solutions" to combat terrorism and organised crime.
Discussions also focused on ensuring security in the cyber, maritime, and energy domains.
The meeting addressed new and emerging threats in the region.
A key outcome was the adoption of guidelines for the maritime component of Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR).
These guidelines will help member states undertake relief operations in the region in an expeditious manner.
The aim is to speed up joint disaster-response operations in the Bay of Bengal region.
The meeting also endorsed a set of guiding principles on the conduct of maritime law enforcement agencies during interactions at sea.
These principles aim to improve safety and predictability during maritime engagements among member countries.
NSA Doval also hosted a series of targeted, private bilateral meetings with his counterparts on 15 July 2026.
India is hosting the BIMSTEC Centre of Excellence for Disaster Management and the BIMSTEC Energy Centre in Bengaluru.
Under various initiatives, 300 youth from BIMSTEC countries will be trained in India every year.
India has also hosted the BIMSTEC Aquatic Championship and will host the BIMSTEC Athletics Meet.
China has undertaken a massive drive to finance and build infrastructure in South and Southeast Asia through the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).
The BRI has a presence in almost all BIMSTEC countries except Bhutan and India.
This has made BIMSTEC more important for India as a counterweight to Chinese influence. BRI –
The Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) is a global development strategy launched by the People's Republic of China in September 2013.
The BRI consists of two primary components: ➢"Silk Road Economic Belt" (land routes) and ➢"21st Century Maritime Silk Road" (sea routes).
As of 2025, over 150 countries — representing nearly 75% of the world's population and over half of global GDP — have joined the BRI.
More than 200 BRI cooperation agreements have been signed with over 150 countries and 30 international organizations.
The BRI includes numerous economic corridors crossing continents, with maritime extensions into the Arctic and the Indo-Pacific.

BRI includes six major economic corridors: ➢China-Mongolia-Russia, ➢New Eurasian Land Bridge, ➢China-Central Asia-West Asia, ➢China-Pakistan (CPEC), ➢Bangladesh-China-India-Myanmar (BCIM), and ➢China-Indochina Peninsula.
The BRI is based on five priorities: policy coordination, facilities connectivity, unimpeded trade, financial integration, and people-to- people bonds.
These priorities guide cooperation across infrastructure, trade, finance, and cultural exchange.
In 2017, the Communist Party of China officially incorporated the advancement of the BRI into its constitution.
